chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Isma'il ibn Marar from Yunus from Ali ibn Yaqteen who said:
I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about shortening (the prayer) in Mecca, so he said, 'Complete it, and it is not obligatory, except that I love for you what I love for myself.'

key_terms.التَّقْصِيرُ: Shortening the prayer (performing 2 rak'ahs instead of 4)
key_terms.مَكَّةَ: Mecca, the city where shortening is not obligatory

ai.seo_question: Is it obligatory to shorten prayer in Mecca according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the ruling on shortening prayers in Mecca is clarified as permissible but not obligatory, highlighting the distinction between legal necessity (wajib) and personal preference (mustahabb). The Imam’s phrase 'I love for you what I love for myself' underscores the Shia concept of *al-walaa'* and the spiritual closeness between the Imam and the believer, encouraging the follower to emulate the Imam’s voluntary acts of worship. This reflects the broader Shia jurisprudential view that while Mecca is exempt from the rule of *qasr*, maintaining the full four-rak'ah prayer remains a highly recommended practice to preserve the integrity of the prayer structure.
